extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, philosophers of mathematics, and users of proof assistants/formalizers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for evaluating mathematical proofs, both informal and formal (including presentation, explanatory power, generality, algorithmic content, and suitability for mechanized verification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof as communicable text / correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is some kind of communicable text (which may involve diagrams) that, in particular, provides sufficient information to establish that the purported theorem is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correctness understood as providing a self-contained warrant that the theorem follows from assumptions; formal axiomatic deduction explicates this notion. Anti-pattern: texts that claim results without supplying enough justificatory information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory power
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof can explain how it might have been discovered, how an associated problem was solved, or why certain features of the statement of the theorem are relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanatory proofs show 'why' as well as 'that' — e.g., they reveal underlying strategies or motivations. Such proofs are valued for pedagogy and conceptual understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength and generality
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs may establish stronger statements than the theorem they purport to prove and may introduce definitions and methods that are useful in other contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer proofs that yield stronger or more general results or that provide methods that transfer to other problems. Example: proofs that suggest generalizations or extend to families of statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fruitfulness / research usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs may suggest solutions to a more general problem, suggest related theorems and questions, or introduce concepts that open new avenues of inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a proof leads to further mathematics (new questions, techniques, or connections). Anti-pattern: isolated proofs that give no insight for further work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic / computational information
rubrics_metrics.description: A good proof can be computationally informative: it may provide explicit algorithms or show how to methodically find witnesses (e.g., algorithms to write primes as sums of squares).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the proof is constructive or can be turned into an explicit algorithm; note tradeoffs where some proofs downplay calculational detail while others provide explicit methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability, memorability, and reconstructability
rubrics_metrics.description: A good proof should be easy to read, easy to remember, and easy to reconstruct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider presentation, clarity of exposition, and whether the argument’s main ideas can be retained and re-derived. Anti-patterns: convoluted presentations that obscure the main idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization and role of lemmas/definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher-level features of the presentation of a proof, such as the organizational role of lemmas and definitions, are relevant to evaluations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how lemmas, definitions, and the decomposition of the argument clarify the strategy and make verification or reuse easier. Good structure filters subordinate representational features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual background and appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluations, with respect to both correctness and other standards of merit, are carried out with respect to appropriate background contexts (assumed resources and knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess proofs relative to the intended audience’s background and available resources (e.g., accepted results, notational conventions). Anti-pattern: demanding use of exotic background without justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of level of detail / informality
rubrics_metrics.description: Informality and the level of detail in a proof are independent features; a proof can be informal and detailed or high-level and still formalizable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the level of detail is suitable for the intended purpose: pedagogical proofs may need more explanation; research announcements may legitimately omit routine inferential details. Anti-pattern: under-detailed arguments that leave crucial inferential gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and explicitness of definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The use and presentation of definitions matter: explicit, well-chosen definitions aid understanding and differentiate between implicit and explicit uses of concepts (e.g., group notion vs. buried set-theoretic encoding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer proofs that make key concepts and uses explicit rather than hiding them behind cumbersome encodings; this supports conceptual analysis and transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of effective conceptual strategies (equivalence, invariants, canonical representatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing an equivalence relation that filters out representational features, assigning suitable invariants, and choosing canonical representatives are valuable strategies in proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the proof employs such strategies to simplify the problem or illuminate structure (e.g., reducing forms to reduced representatives, using discriminants). These strategies often increase generality and explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalizability and mechanized-verification friendliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs that can be expressed in a formal proof language (e.g., Isar/Isabelle, Mizar, Coq) and that fit the goal-refinement model are valuable for mechanized checking and robustness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the high-level structure is explicit enough for translation to proof assistants; follow Isar-style advice: 'Do not manipulate the proof state into a particular form by applying tactics but state the desired form explicitly and let the tactic verify...' — this yields more readable and robust formal proofs. Anti-pattern: informal arguments that resist formal encoding or depend heavily on opaque tactics.
